newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: One-eyed leader heads secretive Taleban.
newsitem.headline: One-eyed leader heads secretive Taleban.

text.p: Here is a profile of the Taleban Islamic militia that took over the Afghanistan capital of Kabul on Friday.

The Taleban has in the past two years swept aside warring guerrilla factions, taken control of most of Afghanistan, hanged its former president from a traffic-control post, and declared it would enforce an Islamic system in the country.

The Taleban movement burst onto the Afghan scene in late 1994 after it was formed by Islamic religious students led by Mullah Muhammad Omar, a former guerrilla fighter who was wounded several times in battles with Soviet soldiers in the 1980s.
Little is known of the one-eyed Mohammad Omar, who according to news reports returned to religious studies after 1989, when the Soviet forces left Afghanistan. He is in his 30s.

Riding a wave of revulsion against local warlords and general weariness over the country's civil war, he and other religious students formed the Taleban and battled Mujahideen guerrilla commanders who had preyed on traders at checkposts in the southern province of Kandahar.
Their ranks grew rapidly, and despite military setbacks in 1995, they proved more united and better disciplined than the faction-ridden government and rival guerrilla groups.

But the Taleban has remained a secretive organisation, revealing little of its structure or political ambitions, and according to news reports out of Afghanistan, its fundamentalism has not always proven popular.
Banning television sets, closing down girls' schools and forcing women to cover their faces, the movement has not always gone down well in areas under its control.

But for the most part, their administration apparently has been relatively efficient, free of the corruption and interference common under other factions, allowing modest commerce to be revived in the war-ravaged country.
How Afghanistan as a whole would thrive under Taleban rule is less certain.
Within hours of their takeover, the militia hanged President Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai from a concrete traffic-control post at the gates of the presidential palace.
The movement also announced that an interim, six-man ruling council would now run the country.

A declaration issued by Mohammad Omar and quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) news service named his deputy, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani (no relation of the president) to head the council.
An earlier statement by Omar carried by AIP declared Afghanistan a "completely Islamic state" where a "complete Islamic system will be enforced."
"A taleban victory in Kabul would have major implications, including a strict enforcement of Islamic law," the London-based Jane's Defence Weekly wrote in March.
It said the movement did not have the power and experience to seize the whole country and maintain law and order.

According to Jane's, writing last year, the movement's central leadership, or shura, is composed of eight members, of whom Mohammad Omar, Mohammad Rabbani, Borjan and Mohammad Abbas are the key players.
Mohammad Rabbani was named governor of the newly captured Nangarhar earlier this month.

Little is known of the others, except most appear to share the background of being born in Kandahar, fighting the Soviet occupation in the 1980s and returning to their religious studies in the wake of the Soviet withdrawal in 1989.
